opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something we think about a lot. The way I see it, there's a real tension between the two systems. System two is the slow, deliberate part: looking at a scene, understanding language, planning in steps, like "go to the fridge, open it, grab the apple." That benefits enormously from big vision-language models trained on internet-scale data, and it can run fairly slowly, maybe a few times a second. System one is the fast, almost subconscious motor control: turning a plan into continuous joint actions, ideally at something like 100 Hz or more, because that's what smooth, reactive, dexterous behavior needs.

So the tradeoff is this. If you split them into separate modules, with an LLM or VLM up top and a separate controller below, each part is easier to engineer and debug. The problem is the interface between them. You're forcing the two to communicate through some hand-designed bottleneck, like text or a fixed set of skills. Language is a very lossy way to describe motion. You can't really express in words exactly how to rotate your wrist to pick up a slippery cup. Information gets lost at that boundary, and errors don't propagate back cleanly during training.

A single model trained end to end gets rid of that bottleneck. Gradients flow all the way from the motor outputs back up into the reasoning layers, so the high-level representations learn what actually matters for control and the low-level policy gets access to rich semantic understanding. That's why with GR00T N1 we went with a dual-system architecture that is still one integrated model. The vision-language part does the slower reasoning, a diffusion transformer generates fast motor actions, and the two are trained together. You get the inductive bias of two speeds and two roles without the brittleness of a hard interface.

There are real costs, though. A monolithic model is harder to interpret. When something fails, it's not always obvious whether it misunderstood the instruction or just fumbled the grasp. It's also expensive to run on the robot's onboard compute at high frequency, which is why the decoupled timescales matter so much. And the biggest constraint is data. End-to-end training needs huge amounts of paired data covering everything from perception to action, and robot data is really scarce. You can't scrape motor control data off the internet.

That's why I think of it as a data pyramid. At the bottom is internet-scale video and text, in the middle is synthetic data from simulation and neural world models, and at the top is a smaller amount of real robot data from teleoperation. A unified model can absorb all of those layers, while a modular system tends to waste a lot of it.

So my bet is that the field moves toward unified models with internal structure, two systems inside one brain. That's roughly how biology does it too. Your cortex and cerebellum work at very different speeds, but they aren't connected by an API. They co-evolved and were trained together. I think robotics will end up in a similar place.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts system two running a few times per second with system one needing roughly 100 Hz, then cites the cost of running the unified model at high frequency as a constraint and explains why decoupled timescales matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, and I'll say upfront that I don't think there's a settled answer yet. The field is genuinely split on it.

Let me first frame what we mean. System two is the slow, deliberate stuff — understanding a language instruction, decomposing a task, reasoning about the scene, deciding that to make a cup of coffee you need to find the mug first. System one is the fast, reflexive stuff — the actual motor control, keeping your balance, adjusting your grip when the object starts to slip. In humans these run on very different timescales and arguably very different substrates. So the question is whether you want one giant model doing both, or a hierarchy where a big VLM does the thinking and a smaller, faster policy does the acting.

The case for the monolithic model is basically the bitter lesson. Every time we've tried to hand-design the boundary between modules, the end-to-end model eventually wins once you have enough data and enough compute. And there's a real cost to having a seam in the architecture. Information has to pass through some bottleneck — a language subgoal, a waypoint, a latent — and you're betting that the bottleneck you designed carries everything the low-level controller needs. Often it doesn't. The high-level planner says "pick up the cup," but the cup is wet, or it's heavier than it looks, and that information lives in the visual and tactile stream that the planner either didn't attend to or couldn't express. A single model with shared representations can in principle let the reasoning layers and the control layers talk to each other in ways you never anticipated.

The case against it, and this is where the engineering reality bites, is latency and sample efficiency. A frontier-scale VLM runs at maybe a few hertz if you're lucky. Low-level control on a humanoid needs to run at fifty, a hundred, sometimes hundreds of hertz. You physically cannot route every control tick through a hundred-billion-parameter model. So even if you philosophically want one model, you end up with something like an asynchronous design — the big model emits a plan or a latent at low frequency, and something smaller consumes it at high frequency. And at that point you've reintroduced the hierarchy whether you call it that or not.

The other thing is data. System two capabilities you can get almost for free from internet-scale pretraining. The model already knows what a kitchen looks like and what a mug is for. System one is the opposite — there's basically no internet data for how to modulate joint torques on your specific robot. That has to come from teleoperation, from simulation, from real-world rollouts. These are wildly different data regimes, and jamming them into one training run means you're constantly fighting about the mixture. Finetune too hard on robot data and you lose the reasoning. Too little and the robot doesn't move well.

So where I've landed, at least for now, is that the right mental model is "one model, two timescales." You want the representation to be shared — the thing that reasons and the thing that acts should see the world through the same eyes. But you want the computation to be factored so that the fast loop doesn't wait on the slow loop. Whether that's literally one network with early-exit heads, or a big model and a small model trained jointly with a learned interface, I think is an implementation detail that will get resolved empirically.

And honestly, my suspicion is that in five years we'll look back and think the question itself was a bit of a false dichotomy. The brain isn't monolithic, but it's also not a clean pipeline. It's a messy, densely connected system where the "modules" are more like regions of emphasis than hard boundaries. I think robot foundation models will converge on something similar — unified at the level of representation and training, heterogeneous at the level of compute and latency.

r001.rationale: The response says a frontier-scale VLM runs at a few hertz while humanoid motor control needs 50–100+ Hz, making it impossible to route every control tick through one huge model.

astra-6.text:
I think the key tradeoff is between integration and specialization. With a monolithic model, you can potentially train everything end to end: perception, reasoning, and action. You don’t have to design an interface where one model expresses an intention and another model translates it into motion. That’s attractive, because information can get lost at that boundary.

But reasoning and motor control operate on very different timescales. If a robot is slipping, it needs to react immediately. It can’t wait for a long chain of reasoning about what went wrong. And you don’t necessarily want to run a huge reasoning model every time you adjust a joint.

So I would lean toward a tightly coupled, hierarchical architecture. System two handles the slower decisions—what am I trying to do, how should I approach it, do I need to replan? System one handles the fast feedback loop. The challenge is making that interface rich enough that you’re not just passing a sentence like ‘pick up the cup’ and hoping the controller figures everything out.

There’s also a distinction between sharing a foundation and sharing an execution loop. You could share representations, or even train the components together, while running them at different frequencies. To me, that’s a promising middle ground: preserve the benefits of joint learning without forcing every motor action through the full reasoning process.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning and motor control operate on different timescales, with fast motor feedback contrasted against slower reasoning, and explains that routing every motor action through the full reasoning process is a drawback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension between the two. System two reasoning benefits from scale and deliberation. If you’re planning how to clean a kitchen, you can afford to spend a few seconds thinking. System one control has a very different constraint: you need to react quickly and consistently. You can’t pause to reason through every token while your robot is losing its balance.

A single model is attractive because everything can be trained together. The reasoning has access to what the robot sees and does, and you avoid some of the information loss that comes from connecting separate modules. But you’re also asking one architecture to operate at very different timescales. Running a huge model for every motor command is expensive, and variable latency becomes a physical problem.

So I would lean toward a hierarchical system: a slower model that understands the task and produces goals, and a fast policy that turns those goals into actions. The important thing is that the connection shouldn’t be purely one-way. The controller needs to feed back when something unexpected happens, so the planner can revise its assumptions.

You could still share representations or train the components jointly. To me, the key distinction isn’t necessarily one model versus two models. It’s whether the system can allocate computation appropriately—think longer when it needs to, and react immediately when it has to.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts deliberative system-two planning, which can take seconds, with system-one control, which must react quickly, and identifies running one model across those different timescales as a difficulty.
